paras: The attempted lynching of Frank Allen took place in Milwaukee, Wisconsin, on the night of September 6, 1882, when a mob fought police officers in an effort to lynch Allen after he was accused of shooting two men in a saloon. The officers secured Allen and he was locked up; the mob's attempt is known from a single wire dispatch, and no report gives the race of anyone involved.

According to a roundup item printed in Wisconsin and Minnesota papers, Allen, described as "of Burlington," quarreled with a regular customer of a Milwaukee saloon and ended the dispute by drawing a revolver and "dispersing the crowd present." A differing brief said Allen had "took too much firewater" and that John Waters and a man named Johnson were shot when they tried to dissuade him. Both versions reported that Waters, a machinist, was fatally wounded and that Charles Johnson was shot in the thigh or leg.

A Milwaukee dispatch dated September 7 and printed in the Wheeling Register said that officers secured Allen only after a hard fight with a mob "determined to lynch him." Neither of the other versions mentions a mob, saying only that Allen was "finally subdued and locked up."
No report of an inquest into Waters's death, or of a trial of Allen, appears in the coverage.

The Wheeling Register ran the story on September 8 under the headlines "A Desperado" and "Cleans Out a Saloon and Shoots Two Men," presenting the mob's effort without comment. Later in the week the shooting appeared as one item in crime columns, "A Tragical Record" in the Mower County Transcript and Brookings County Sentinel and a similar list in the Watertown Republican, none of which mentioned the mob. The Batesville Guard in Arkansas carried a jocular version among its "Late News Items," with Allen going "on the war-path with a revolver," and the same brief ran in the Phillipsburg Herald in Kansas and the Grenada Sentinel in Mississippi.
None of these papers identified the race of Allen, his victims or the crowd, and no Black-press coverage from 1882 is available.
The accounts differ on how the shooting began, a quarrel with a saloon regular in one version and drunken rampage in the other, and only the Wheeling dispatch reports an attempted lynching.

framing.detail: The Wheeling Register ran the dispatch under 'A Desperado' and 'Cleans Out a Saloon and Shoots Two Men,' treating the would-be lynchers without comment.
Roundups in Wisconsin, Minnesota and Dakota papers listed the shooting among crimes of the week without mention of a mob.
The Batesville Guard's brief joked that Allen 'took too much firewater' and 'went on the war-path.'
